title: Enrolments in five batches
intro: A coaching institute runs five batches, A, B, C, D and E. The table shows the number of students who enrolled in each batch in each of four months, with each batch's four-month total and each month's total over all five batches. Eight entries are missing.
Additional information is given below the table.
clues: Each of the 20 monthly figures in the table (excluding the totals), including each missing one, is a multiple of 5 from 10 to 60, inclusive.
In each month, no two batches had the same number of enrolments.
Batch C's enrolments rose every month.
In April, batch B had the second-highest number of enrolments.

questions.stem: How many students enrolled in batch D in January?
why: C's row: 15 + Feb + 35 + Apr = 125, so Feb + Apr = 75, with 15 < Feb < 35 < Apr (fact 3). As multiples of 5 within 10 to 60, (Feb, Apr) is (20, 55) or (25, 50).
April's column: 25 + B + C + D + 35 = 205, so B + C + D = 145 in April. B's row gives B Feb + B Apr = 95, and D's row gives D Jan + D Apr = 95.

Try C = 50 in April: then B + D = 95. If B is 45 or less, D is 50 or more, so C and D both stand above B. If B is 55 or more, D is 40 or less and B is the highest. B = 50 ties with C. None leaves B second (facts 2 and 4). So C = 55, and B + D = 90 with B second: B = 50, D = 40.
So C's February is 20, and D's January is 95 − 40 = 55.

questions.stem: In how many of the four months did batch E have more enrolments than batch A?
why: January's column: A + 25 + 15 + 55 + 30 = 165 gives A Jan = 40, and A's row then gives A Feb = 150 − 40 − 50 − 25 = 35.
E is ahead in February and April only: 2 months.

questions.stem: What percentage of all April enrolments was accounted for by batches B and D together, to the nearest integer?
why: In April, B had 50 and D had 40, out of 205 in all.
90 ÷ 205 = 43.9%, which is 44 to the nearest integer.

questions.stem: Taking each batch's best month, what was the highest share of a batch's own four-month total enrolled in a single month?
why: Each batch's largest month over its own total: A 50 of 150 (33.3%), B 50 of 150 (33.3%), C 55 of 125 (44.0%), D 55 of 145 (37.9%), E 50 of 160 (31.3%).
D also had 55 in a month, but over a larger total: the largest single entry is not the largest share.

questions.stem: If the information in point 4 were not available, and everything else stayed the same, which of the following could NOT be batch B's enrolment in February?
why: Without fact 4, the totals and facts 1 to 3 allow four ways to fill the table, and B's February entry is 40, 45 or 55 in them.

B Feb = 35 would need A Feb + C Feb = 180 − 35 − 30 − 50 = 65 and B Apr = 150 − 25 − 30 − 35 = 60. Working through C's two options, either D's January leaves the 10 to 60 range or D's April becomes 35, tying with E's April.
So 35 is the one value B's February entry cannot take. 40, 45 and 55 each appear in a fill that keeps every fact but the fourth.

steps: Write each row's and column's missing sum first. A: Jan + Feb = 75. B: Feb + Apr = 95. C: Feb + Apr = 75. D: Jan + Apr = 95. January: A + D = 95. February: A + B + C = 100. April: B + C + D = 145.
Batch C rises every month (fact 3): 15 < Feb < 35 < Apr with Feb + Apr = 75, so (Feb, Apr) is (20, 55) or (25, 50).
Fact 4 settles April: B must be second-highest, so C takes 55 and B 50, and D gets 145 − 105 = 40. Then C Feb = 20.
Every other blank follows from a sum: B Feb = 95 − 50 = 45, D Jan = 95 − 40 = 55, A Jan = 95 − 55 = 40, A Feb = 75 − 40 = 35.
Check fact 2, month by month: January 40, 25, 15, 55, 30; February 35, 45, 20, 30, 50; March 50, 30, 35, 20, 45; April 25, 50, 55, 40, 35. No ties: the table fills exactly one way.
